live.name: ALPHV
live.headline: ALPHV: a ransomware actor known by several names
live.in_short: The catalogue lists ALPHV under several aliases and a set of tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: ALPHV is the main name for this actor in the catalogue record.
It is also listed as ALPHVM, Ambitious Scorpius, BlackCat Gang and UNC4466.
The catalogue links the name to tools including BlackCat, Noberus, Munchkin, Mimikatz, Impacket, PsExec, LaZagne, MEGAsync and GO Simple Tunnel (GOST).
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: ALPHV
next.headline: ALPHV (BlackCat): a ransomware-as-a-service gang that hit casinos, county governments and health firms
next.in_short: ALPHV, also called BlackCat, ran a ransomware-as-a-service operation from late 2021. Reporters tied it to attacks on MGM, Suffolk County and Henry Schein. Reports say it went dark in March 2024, which BleepingComputer called an exit scam.

sentences.t: ALPHV is also tracked as ALPHVM, Ambitious Scorpius, BlackCat Gang and UNC4466.
Cybernews says the ransomware was first seen in late 2021, and Sygnia says the group surfaced in November 2021.
BleepingComputer reports that ALPHV is believed to be a rebrand of the DarkSide and BlackMatter ransomware operations.
Cybernews and Sygnia both describe a ransomware-as-a-service business. Cybernews says the group sells malware subscriptions to criminals, and notes that the ransomware was written in Rust.
BleepingComputer says the FBI estimates the group took at least $300 million in ransom payments from more than 1,000 victims up to September 2023.

Victims named in the reports are a mixed group. They include local governments such as Suffolk County and the city of Alexandria, a casino operator, a dental and medical distributor, a mortgage lender and a Canadian software company.
Sygnia describes the group as targeting high-profile organisations across many sectors, worldwide.
In a 2023 case, Sygnia attributed an attack to BlackCat or one of its affiliates. Initial access came through a compromised third-party vendor.
In that case the attacker moved sideways over several weeks using Cobalt Strike and proxy tools. It copied data out with Rclone and then sent extortion emails to employees.
The catalogue record lists tools tied to ALPHV, including Mimikatz, PsExec, Impacket, LaZagne and MEGAsync.

ALPHV's own account of the MGM attack says it kept super administrator access to the victim's Okta system. It also says it sniffed passwords on Okta Agent servers. These are the gang's claims and are unverified.

CrowdStrike says ransomware-as-a-service platforms including Alphv were used against VMware ESXi hypervisors in early 2023. ALPHV says it launched ransomware against more than 100 ESXi hypervisors at MGM.
The group runs a leak site and pairs it with threats. In one claim it said stolen data would be released in stages every 12 hours.
ReliaQuest says Scattered Spider gains access through alliances with ransomware operators including ALPHV. Check Point lists BlackCat/ALPHV among the tools noted for Scattered Spider.

In September 2022, DataBreaches reported that BlackCat claimed the attack that disabled Suffolk County's 911 system. The group claimed 400 GB of county and contractor data, which the publisher could not confirm.
Also in September 2022, Cybernews reported that BlackCat listed the IT firm NJVC on its leak site and then removed the entry. The breach is the gang's own claim.
In September 2023, ALPHV posted its own account of the MGM Resorts attack. The article does not independently verify it.
A report says AlphV claimed the Henry Schein incident and re-encrypted systems after negotiations broke down.
In December 2023, BleepingComputer reports, an international law enforcement operation seized the gang's Tor negotiation and leak sites. The report calls the disruption temporary.
Also in December 2023, DataBreaches reported an unconfirmed claim by AlphV. The group said it got a Viking Therapeutics employee to file an SEC complaint about the breach.
In February 2024, unnamed sources told BleepingComputer the group was linked to the Change Healthcare attack. BleepingComputer could not confirm this, and BlackCat had not claimed it at the time.
UnitedHealth's SEC filing said a nation-state threat actor was behind that attack. BleepingComputer notes that BlackCat has not been publicly linked to any foreign government agencies.
The U.S. State Department offered rewards of up to $10 million for information on ALPHV's leaders, and $5 million for information on individuals linked to its attacks.
In March 2024, BleepingComputer concluded the gang was running an exit scam. Its sites went offline, affiliates said they were not paid, and it offered its source code for $5 million.

The gang posted a fake FBI seizure banner. Europol and the NCA said they were not involved, and the FBI declined to comment. BleepingComputer says it is unclear whether the group will return under a new name.
Check what access outside vendors hold on your network, and keep backups out of reach of everyday domain accounts.
Treat a gang's leak-site claims as unconfirmed until the victim or an investigator verifies them.
